articles.title: World: Primary health care-oriented responses for migrants, refugees and displaced populations
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. WHO calls for migrant-inclusive primary health care to strengthen health systems for all The World Health Organization (WHO) has launched the eighth report in the Global Evidence Review on Health and Migration (GEHM) series, Primary health care-oriented responses for migrants, refugees and displaced populations. Developed by the WHO Health and Migration Programme in collaboration with WHO’s Service Delivery and Primary Health Care Unit, the report examines how primary health care-oriented responses can improve access, continuity and quality of care for people on the move, while strengthening health systems for diverse populations. “Reaching people on the move is integral to achieving health for all. Health systems designed to reach those facing the greatest barriers are ultimately stronger, more equitable and more resilient for everyone,” said Dr Santino Severoni, Head of the WHO Health and Migration Programme. Evidence points to promising approaches, but major gaps remain The review screened 2901 records and synthesized evidence from 37 publications. It found that primary health care-oriented responses can improve first contact with care through affordable services, language support, community outreach and service design. They can strengthen continuity and coordination through navigators, referral pathways, multidisciplinary teams and partnerships across health, social and community services. PHC-oriented responses were most effective when integrated services, workforce support and relationships with communities worked together. These mutually reinforcing mechanisms can be strengthened progressively, building on capacities and adapting to context. Even partially integrated or resource-constrained programmes produced meaningful improvements in access, trust, service use and community engagement. However, the evidence remains uneven. Most studies were conducted in high-income countries, while labour migrants and undocumented migrants were rarely represented. Evidence was limited on financing and sustainability, phases of migration, health information systems, emergency preparedness, timeliness, safety and people-centredness. Locally generated evidence and innovations from low- and middle-income and resource-constrained settings remain under-documented. “Migrant health should not be treated as a separate or parallel area of service delivery. It offers a practical lens through which to assess how well health systems are delivering on the vision of primary health care,” said Dr Kalipso Chalkidou, Director of WHO’s Department of Performance, Financing and Delivery. “The challenge is to embed what works into policies, financing arrangements and service-delivery models, so that promising responses become sustained institutional practice.” From evidence to implementation Placing inclusion at the heart of primary health care is essential to advancing health equity, universal health coverage and the right to health for all. The report calls on policymakers to embed effective approaches within national health systems, strengthen multisectoral coordination and support implementation at national and subnational levels. The discussion highlighted the need to: integrate effective responses into national health systems while retaining features tailored to population needs; support culturally responsive care, interpretation, workforce capacity and community-based roles; strengthen multisectoral coordination, sustainable financing and links across national, regional and local levels; develop ethical, disaggregated health information systems that measure needs and outcomes while maintaining separation between health and immigration data; generate actionable evidence through collaboration among policy-makers, practitioners, researchers and people with lived experience; document and share innovations from low- and middle-income and resource-constrained settings; and involve migrants, refugees and displaced communities, including young people, in designing and evaluating services.
